subsystems.name: Crypto abstraction layer
subsystems.role: the single place where an algorithm is chosen and invoked, so applications never call crypto primitives directly.

subsystems.name: Cryptographic inventory and discovery
subsystems.role: find every place crypto is used, including firmware, configs and certificates, so you know what must change.

subsystems.name: Key and certificate management
subsystems.role: issue, rotate and revoke keys without editing application code.
parts: hardware security modules or key management service

subsystems.name: Negotiation and policy engine
subsystems.role: pick an algorithm at run time and allow old and new peers to talk during a migration.
parts: hybrid modes offering classical and post-quantum algorithms together

subsystems.name: Protocol and data-format layer
subsystems.role: carry algorithm identifiers and dual signatures so stored and transmitted data stays readable across a change.
parts: algorithm identifiers in message and file formats
re-encryption and re-signing paths for archived data

subsystems.name: Test and verification harness
subsystems.role: prove a swap works, is fast enough and still meets compliance rules before it reaches production.

buildSteps.title: Discover and inventory
buildSteps.detail: Scan source code, build artefacts, appliances, embedded devices and certificates for algorithms, key lengths, protocols and expiry. Record who owns each use.

buildSteps.title: Classify data and set policy
buildSteps.detail: Decide which data must stay confidential for how long, since long-lived secrets are the ones quantum computers threaten first. Write down which algorithms are acceptable and until when.

buildSteps.title: Define a stable interface
buildSteps.detail: Wrap every cryptographic operation behind a narrow internal API that takes the algorithm as an explicit parameter, and remove hardcoded algorithm choices from business logic.

buildSteps.title: Centralise keys and certificates
buildSteps.detail: Move keys into hardware security modules or a managed key service, and automate issuance, rotation and revocation so a change of algorithm is a configuration change.

buildSteps.title: Add negotiation and hybrid modes
buildSteps.detail: Make each endpoint offer several algorithm suites at once, including hybrids that combine a classical and a post-quantum algorithm, so peers running different versions still interoperate.

buildSteps.title: Build the test harness
buildSteps.detail: Assemble test vectors, interoperability tests and benchmarks, plus canary deployments and a switch that reverts to the previous algorithm within minutes.

buildSteps.title: Rehearse a real swap
buildSteps.detail: Run an actual algorithm change on a live but non-critical service, measure how long it takes and what breaks, then fix the process rather than just the service.

buildSteps.title: Keep it continuous
buildSteps.detail: Re-scan on every build, alert when inventory drifts, and review policy whenever standards or threat estimates change.

prerequisites.why: you need agreed, vetted replacements before any swap is worth rehearsing; NIST published ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA in 2024.

prerequisites.tech: Hybrid key exchange in mainstream protocols
prerequisites.why: large web browsers and some servers already negotiate a classical plus post-quantum key exchange, but support is uneven across the rest of the stack.

prerequisites.tech: Hardware security modules and key services with post-quantum support
prerequisites.why: many deployed modules cannot generate or store the new key types, so agility stalls at the hardware boundary until firmware or appliances are replaced.
without an accurate inventory you cannot know how large the migration is; scanners and the cryptographic bill of materials format are still maturing.

prerequisites.tech: Certificate and protocol formats that carry new signature types
prerequisites.why: a swap that is invisible to applications still needs chains, signatures and identifiers that peers can parse.

pathway.milestone: inventory cryptographic assets and put keys under central, automated management
pathway.unlocks: a map of what must change and a way to rotate anything without a code release.

pathway.milestone: hybrid key exchange and composite signatures in production on internet-facing services
pathway.unlocks: protection against store-now-decrypt-later attacks while the newer algorithms prove themselves.

pathway.milestone: rehearsed, routine algorithm swaps on live systems
pathway.unlocks: migration times measured in weeks rather than years, and confidence that a future break can be answered quickly.

pathway.milestone: cryptography treated as a versioned, continuously updated dependency
pathway.unlocks: systems that survive the next algorithm change — and whatever comes after it — without re-architecting.
